landing.typesTitle: Which loft conversion suits your roof?
landing.typesIntro: The right conversion depends on your roof shape, head height and budget. These are the four we build, with honest guide prices, Jason will tell you at the first visit which one your roof actually needs.

types.name: Dormer
types.text: The most popular conversion we build. A flat-roof dormer extends out from the rear slope of the roof, giving you full head height across most of the new room, and usually falls under permitted development.
types.imageAlt: Contemporary clad dormer loft conversion, front elevation

types.name: Hip-to-gable
types.text: Built for semis and end-of-terrace homes with a hipped (sloping) side roof. We build the side wall up into a vertical gable, often paired with a rear dormer, to unlock loft space a hipped roof wastes.
types.imageAlt: Hip-to-gable loft conversion with tiled dormer and rooflights

types.name: Mansard
types.text: The maximum-space option, common on period terraces. The whole rear slope is rebuilt at a near-vertical angle, effectively adding a full extra storey. Usually needs planning permission, which we'll guide you through.
types.imageAlt: Mansard loft conversion on a period terrace

types.name: Velux / rooflight
types.text: If your loft already has generous head height, rooflights and a proper staircase may be all it needs. No change to the roofline, no planning permission in most cases, and the quickest build of the four.
types.imageAlt: Converted loft bedroom with built-in wardrobes

faqs.q: How much does a loft conversion cost?
faqs.a: Most loft conversions we build come in between £45,000 and £75,000. A rear dormer with a bedroom and en-suite typically sits in the middle of that range; a Velux conversion less, a full mansard more. You'll get an exact itemised figure before work starts, and unless you change the scope mid-build, that's the figure you pay.

faqs.q: Do I need planning permission for a loft conversion?
faqs.a: Usually not. Most dormer, hip-to-gable and Velux conversions fall under permitted development rights, so no planning application is needed. Mansards and homes in conservation areas are the main exceptions. Jason will tell you where you stand at the first site visit, before you spend anything.

faqs.q: Is my loft actually suitable for conversion?
faqs.a: The main test is head height, around 2.2m from the top of the ceiling joists to the ridge is the usual benchmark. Roof shape and the position of the stairs matter too. Jason measures all of this at the first visit and will tell you straight if a conversion doesn't make sense for your roof.

faqs.q: How long does a loft conversion take?
faqs.a: Typically 8–12 weeks on site. We agree the schedule with you before we start, and keeping to it is part of the deal. Most of the structural work happens from outside via scaffolding, so disruption inside your home is kept to a minimum until the staircase goes in.

faqs.q: Will I need to move out during the build?
faqs.a: No. Almost all of our clients stay at home throughout. The loft is sealed off from the rest of the house and accessed externally for most of the build, the messiest day is usually when the new staircase is cut through, and we plan that with you in advance.

landing.typesIntro: Four types cover almost every home we work on. These guide prices are for the full build, structure, glazing, first and second fix, plastered and decorated, so you can compare like for like.

types.name: Single-storey rear
types.text: The classic open-plan kitchen-diner. We extend into the garden, open the back of the house with bifold or sliding doors, and bring light deep into the plan with rooflights. Most fall under permitted development.
types.imageAlt: Single-storey rear extension with bifold doors

types.name: Double-storey
types.text: The best cost per square metre of any extension, the foundations and roof are shared across two floors. A bigger kitchen below, an extra bedroom or bathroom above. Needs planning permission, which we'll guide you through.
types.imageAlt: Double-storey rear extension with anthracite bifold doors

types.name: Wraparound
types.text: A rear and side-return extension combined into one L-shaped space. The biggest transformation you can make to the ground floor of a terraced or semi-detached home, one large, light room across the full width.
types.imageAlt: Wraparound rear extension with bifold doors

types.name: Side return
types.text: The Victorian terrace favourite. That dark alley beside your kitchen becomes part of the room, a modest footprint gain that completely changes how the kitchen feels, especially with a glazed roof over the new space.

landing.costRangeNote: Most extensions we build, full build cost
landing.costText: Where you sit in that range depends on size, whether it's one storey or two, and the specification of glazing and finishes. Before work starts you'll have an itemised quotation showing exactly where every pound goes, never a vague day rate or a moving target.
included: Groundworks, foundations and all structural work including steels
Roofing, glazing, bifold or sliding doors and rooflights
First and second fix electrics and plumbing
Plastering, insulation to current regs, and decoration
A build schedule with a start date and a finish date, agreed before we begin

faqs.q: How much does an extension cost?
faqs.a: Most extensions we build come in between £55,000 and £120,000. A straightforward single-storey rear extension sits at the lower end; a double-storey or wraparound at the upper end. You'll get an exact itemised figure before work starts, and unless you change the scope mid-build, that's the figure you pay.

faqs.q: Do I need planning permission for an extension?
faqs.a: Many single-storey rear and side-return extensions fall under permitted development rights, so no planning application is needed. Double-storey extensions and larger schemes usually do need permission. Jason will tell you where you stand at the first site visit, and we'll point you to the right people for drawings and applications.

faqs.q: How long does an extension take to build?
faqs.a: Typically 10–16 weeks on site depending on size and complexity. We agree the schedule with you before we start, and keeping to it is part of the deal, not a nice-to-have.

faqs.q: Can I live in the house during the build?
faqs.a: Yes, nearly all of our clients do. We seal the work area off from the rest of the house and keep water and electrics running to your kitchen for as long as physically possible. The few days where disruption is unavoidable, we plan with you in advance.

faqs.q: Will an extension add value to my home?
faqs.a: A well-built kitchen extension is consistently one of the highest-value improvements you can make, agents typically value the added space at more than a properly priced build costs. More importantly, you get a home that works for how you actually live, without moving.
